newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown to keep inflation goal at Mansion House.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown to keep inflation goal at Mansion House.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will play safe and retain the current inflation target of 2.5 percent or less when he delivers his first Mansion House speech on Thursday, analysts say. They believe the government has little to gain from toughening up or relaxing the target, and any change in the measure of inflation used would add more confusion than clarity.
"I can't see any advantage either way in changing the target," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.

"If the Chancellor raises the target or makes any other changes interpreted as a relaxation he will lose credibility on inflation and the long end of the gilt market, which has seen average yields fall, will suffer."

Brown won his anti-inflation spurs within days of taking office when he granted the Bank of the England power to set interest rates independently. Inflation expectations, as measured by the yields of long-dated government bonds, fell dramatically the same day.

But Mackie said to introduce a tougher target at this stage would have limited benefits too. "Brown has already put on enough of a monetary hair shirt by giving the Bank independence. I can't see what he gains by trying to be even tougher."
The Chancellor's annual Mansion House speech has become a key event in the City diary and has in recent years been used to unveil new twists in monetary policy.
Britain first adopted the target for underlying inflation (RPIX), which excludes mortgage interest payments, when the pound was ejected from the Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992.
It consisted of a one to four percent band, with the target the midpoint or below by the end of the parliament. The band was more or less abandoned two years ago by former Chancellor Kenneth Clarke.
Inflation managed to meet the target for the first time in almost three years in April when it fell to 2.5 percent, the last month of the Parliament.
But it came too late for Clarke. By the time the figures were released in May, he had already lost his job and taken a seat on the opposition benches after Labour's massive victory on May 1.
The new Chancellor, however, has shown a willingness for dramatic chance and could choose to surprise financial markets by abandoning RPIX in favour of another measure.

There are two contenders to replace it: RPIY, retail prices excluding mortgage interest payments and indirect taxes; and EU harmonised CPI, retail prices excluding owner occupied housing, education fees and health care.
Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe, said while a change to either of these two measures would bring material benefits, it carries the risk of being interpreted as a softer option.
Both measures run below RPIX. RPIY was 2.0 percent in the year to April and harmonised CPI 1.6 percent.
"Such a move would suggest marginally less upward pressure on base rates," he said.
Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc, said the Chancellor could also catch markets on the hop and reintroduce a lower limit of, for example, 1.0 percent.

"The advantage of that would be to point out that undershooting the target could be a negative. But since we have struggled to meet 2.5 percent since the target was introduced, a lower limit at this stage seems a little premature."

Most economists agreed financial markets would welcome some continuity at a time when much of the framework has been swept away. "Any change that makes the target look easier to meet will be regarded very cynically by bond markets and on the foreign exchanges," said Shaw.

And Mackie said there is such a thing as too much tinkering. "My advice would be to leave the inflation target alone, stick with the current level and measure despite its imperfections and let the new system settle in."
